porbos.title: Those Who Gave Up Everything to Search • Those Whose Lives Were Spent in Waiting • From ‘Adnan to Hashim • ‘Abd al-Muttalib, Zamzam and the Vow

blocks.0: Those Who Gave Up Everything to Search
blocks.1: In the last lesson we entered the darkness of Jahili Arabia. Idols, blood-vengeance, buried daughters, people sold.
blocks.2: Even in that darkness there were a few people who did not keep their eyes closed. Today we begin with them.
blocks.3: Everyone bows his head before a stone; they did not bow. Everyone eats meat slaughtered in the name of idols; they would not put it to their mouths. People said, these are mad. They had a name; hanif. And one word in their hearts; someone will come.
blocks.4: In the shade of the northern wall of the Ka‘bah an old man stands with his back against it. His name is Zayd ibn ‘Amr. The crowd of the tawaf flows past him. Someone is touching al-Lat, someone al-‘Uzza. He touches no one. Raising his face, he says, O Allah! If I knew the path You love most, I would worship You on that path. But I do not know. He says this every day. No one listens.
blocks.5: It was a few years ago. In the gathering of the Quraysh he had said, the sheep was made by Allah, the grass was grown by Allah, the water was sent down by Allah. And you slaughter in another’s name! The gathering fell silent. Then his own uncle stood up. He said, leave Makkah. We do not want to see your face any more. Since then his address has been Mount Hira. A man, a cave, and a face raised towards the sky.
blocks.6: One day he took the road to Syria with his camels. Monks, rabbis, whoever was wherever; one question to all. Where is the religion of Ibrahim? At last a scholar said, what you are searching for exists nowhere else. But in your own land a prophet will come. The time has come. Run. Zayd turned the camel’s head around. One word inside his chest; just a few more days. I will return to my land and take that hand.
blocks.7: The road did not end. Near the border of Syria bandits fell upon him. The man who spent his whole life searching for a prophet collapsed on the desert sand without seeing that prophet’s face. Prophethood was then within reach. Only a few years away.{{1}}
blocks.8: Many years later the Prophet {{1}} was asked about Zayd. He said, on the plain of Resurrection he will rise as a whole Ummah by himself.
blocks.9: In another corner of Makkah, another old man. A cousin of Khadijah (RA). His name was Waraqah ibn Nawfal. He too had one day given up the idols. Then he went and sat with the Christians. At this age he learned Hebrew. And with trembling hands he sat and copied the Torah and the Injil; page after page.
blocks.10: Years rolled on. The light of his eyes went out little by little. Now he no longer sees letters. His back has bent. Yet if anyone sits beside him he says that one thing. A prophet will come to this people. If I live until that day; with these blind eyes, with this bent back, I will fight for him.{{1}}
blocks.11: A whole life passed in this one sentence. He did get that day. Somehow. At the very last moment. After the first revelation he lived only a few more days. The story of those few days is in the next lesson.
blocks.12: The third had come from so far away that listening to his story makes the heart heavy. His name is Salman. His country, Persia. A village near Isfahan. The son of a great landowner. He was the apple of his father’s eye.
blocks.13: He loved him so much that he would not let him set foot outside the house.
blocks.14: Salman (RA) himself said later, my father kept me shut in the house, the way a girl is kept.
blocks.15: He had only one fear. That the boy might be lost. In one corner of the house a fire burned always. Not letting it go out was Salman’s task.
blocks.16: One day his father sent him to work in the field. On the way, a church. From inside, the tune of prayer floated out. Salman stopped. Then went in. He sat there until sunset; he forgot the field. In the evening his father asked, where were you? Salman said, I saw something, father. It is better than our religion.
blocks.17: His father’s face hardened. That very night an iron fetter was put on Salman’s foot. After some days a caravan came from Syria. In the darkness of night Salman undid the fetter and fled. He took nothing with him. Not house, not land, not even that maddening affection of his father.
blocks.18: Going to Syria he took up the service of a monk. But the man was a hypocrite; he piled the people’s charity into his own chest. When he died Salman told everything; people hung his corpse up and stoned it. Then came a new monk. This time a truly good man. Salman loved him like a father. That monk too one day lay on his deathbed. Salman took his hand and said, when you are gone, to whom shall I go? He named a name. A man of Mosul.
blocks.19: Salman went to Mosul. That man too died; before dying he gave another name. Nisibis. The man of Nisibis too died; another name, ‘Ammuriyyah. From one city to another. One old man dies, sends him to another. Salman ties up his bundle again, sets out on the road again. In this way his black hair turned grey.
blocks.20: When the last scholar of ‘Ammuriyyah too lay on his deathbed, Salman asked that same question again. This time he said, my son, no one is left today upon the pure religion. But a time has come. A prophet will come any moment now; with the religion of Ibrahim. He will come to a land of date palms, with fields of black stone on both sides. You will know him by three things. He does not eat charity, he eats a gift. Between his two shoulders is the seal of prophethood. If you can, reach that land.
blocks.21: After some time some Arab merchants were passing that way. Whatever Salman had; a few cows, a few sheep; he put it all in their hands. The condition was only one. Take me to Arabia. They took the goods. Then in the middle of the road they bound Salman. They sold him as a slave to a Jew and went away.
blocks.22: Passing from hand to hand, Salman arrived at one place. Rows of date palms all around. In the distance on two sides, fields of black stone. Salman’s heart leapt. This is that land! But he was then a slave. All day he climbed date palms, picked dates, took the scolding of his master. The dream so near; yet hands and feet bound.
blocks.23: Then one day, sitting up in a tree, he heard. Below, two men were talking; someone has come from Makkah, calling himself a prophet, he has alighted at Quba’. Salman began to tremble. He almost fell from the tree. Coming down he asked, what did you say? Say it again! The master struck him a blow on the back. He said, mind your work.
blocks.24: That evening Salman took some dates he had saved and went to Quba’. Placing them before the Prophet {{1}} he said, this is charity. The Prophet {{2}} said to the Companions, you eat. He did not put even one in his own mouth. In Salman’s heart the first sign rang.
blocks.25: The next day some more dates. This time he said, this is a gift. The Prophet {{1}} stretched out his hand and ate himself too. The second sign. Now the one remaining. Salman went and stood behind the Prophet {{2}}. His eyes on the shoulder. The Prophet {{3}} understood. Saying nothing he moved his cloak a little aside. There; exactly between the two shoulders; a mark like a pigeon’s egg.
blocks.26: Salman could no longer stand. He bent over that mark. He began to kiss it. And began to weep.{{1}}
blocks.27: That boy of Persia; who gave up his father’s affection, gave up his country, wore the fetter, became a slave, turned his hair grey going from one city to another; today he has reached his destination. With his head on a seal.
blocks.28: Even so the story does not end here. Salman was still a slave. Because of this slavery he stayed at home on the day of Badr. And on the day of Uhud. At last the Prophet {{1}} himself stood up. A price was settled with the master; three hundred date saplings and some gold. Then Salman would be free. The Prophet {{2}} sat on the ground. With his own hands he planted three hundred saplings one by one. Not one died. That day Salman became free. For the man who had spent his whole life losing everything in search of freedom, the saplings of his freedom were planted by the Messenger of Allah {{3}}, may Allah’s peace and blessings be upon him, in person.
blocks.29: Three people. One searched page by page of the books. One walked from land to land. Another with his back against the wall of the Ka‘bah, his face raised to the sky. However thick the darkness, Allah keeps some lamps lit.
blocks.32: Even in the man who runs after money all his life, the question one day wakes: is this all?
blocks.33: The boy who stares all night at the light of his mobile phone, at dawn his chest feels empty.
blocks.34: This very feeling of emptiness is the beginning of searching.
blocks.35: Salman (RA) did not suppress this feeling of emptiness; he ran after it.
blocks.36: And when we feel empty, we put on another video.
blocks.37: Those Whose Lives Were Spent in Waiting
blocks.38: These few in Makkah were searching for the truth. But those who had the most news of the truth were someone else.
blocks.39: The name of Madinah was then Yathrib. A few Jewish tribes lived there; Banu Qurayzah, Banu al-Nadir, Banu Qaynuqa‘.
blocks.40: These were not people of this land. Long ago, from far away, they had come here. With camels loaded, crossing the desert, with their families.
blocks.41: Why had they come? It was written in their book that the last prophet would come in a land of date palms, with fields of black stone on both sides. Matching that description they had searched and searched and built their homes in this very Yathrib.
blocks.42: Fathers told sons, he will come. Perhaps in my lifetime, or else in yours. The son, grown up, told his own son the same thing. Generation after generation they lived holding this one hope in their chests.
blocks.43: When a quarrel broke out with the Arabs around them they would say, wait. The time of the prophet has come near. When he comes we will join him and wipe you out like ‘Ad and Iram.
blocks.44: Then he truly came. In that very land of date palms. The signs written in the book matched one after another. They even recognised him; as one recognises one’s own son. But having recognised him, they could not accept him.
blocks.45: Why could they not? Because they had held that the prophet would come from their own lineage; from Bani Isra’il. And this one came from an Arab house, in the line of Isma‘il (AS). After so many ages of waiting, the man was not ‘one of theirs’; with this one fact everything collapsed. Envy, pride of lineage and stubbornness; the three together shut their eyes.
blocks.47: And when there came to them a Book from Allah confirming what they had, although before that they used to pray for victory over the disbelievers; then when there came to them what they recognised, they denied it.{{1}}
blocks.48: What did they lose! Houses, country, the graves of forefathers; leaving all, they had come to this land only for one man. And when he came and stood at the door, they themselves turned their faces away. So great a wait, so small a heart.
blocks.49: There were many others waiting. In a church by the road to Syria an old monk used to come to the door every day; he searched the crowd of the caravan for a face with the signs written in the book. In this way his hair had turned white, his eyes had worn away. The face did not come.
blocks.50: At the fair of ‘Ukaz, sitting on a camel, the old Qus ibn Sa‘idah would cry out, surely Allah has a religion that is better than this religion of yours. And the time for a prophet to come has drawn near.{{1}}
blocks.51: The people in the crowd listened, laughed, forgot. Yet many years later the Prophet {{1}} would say, I saw Qus ibn Sa‘idah at the fair of ‘Ukaz. May Allah have mercy on him.
blocks.52: The book of the Jews was saying, he will come. The Christian monk was watching the caravan, he will come. The old man of the fair was crying out, he will come. The hanifs of Makkah, with their backs against the wall of the Ka‘bah, waiting, he will come.
blocks.53: Not only the heavens. The earth too waited holding its breath.
blocks.54: But the turn of waiting has not ended.
blocks.55: The Prophet {{1}} has said, one will come.
blocks.56: If only a single day of the world’s life remains, Allah will lengthen that day until He sends on that day a man from my family.{{1}}
blocks.57: He will fill the earth with justice and fairness.
blocks.58: The Mahdi is from my family. He will fill the earth with justice and fairness, as it had been filled with oppression and tyranny.{{1}}
blocks.59: The earth that today is full of oppression, on that very earth Allah’s law will stand again.
blocks.60: So even today people look for him. Even today many sit watching the road.
blocks.61: When he will come, no one knows. Nor is anyone meant to know.
blocks.63: Those who in every age sat down to count the days have all been proved false.
blocks.64: That old man of ‘Ukaz did not count days. He only kept his face turned in the right direction.
blocks.65: The monk of Syria did not count days either. He only went every day and stood at the door.
blocks.66: Neither of the two got that day.
blocks.67: Yet until their last day their faces did not turn.
blocks.68: So the question is not this, when will he come.
blocks.69: The question is, on the day he comes, which way will I be standing facing!
blocks.71: Let the story of those whose waiting I spoke of rest here.
blocks.72: Then one day Allah turned and looked. At this forgotten people of the sand; whose name was in no empire’s register, whom no one counted.
blocks.73: He had mercy. And from among them, from one house of theirs, He chose one man.
blocks.74: The one for whom the heavens had waited all this time, for whom the earth had sat holding its breath all this time; he came. The turn of the world’s waiting ended.
blocks.75: Now let us come to that man. First his house, his lineage.
blocks.76: Ibrahim (AS) who built the Ka‘bah, his son was Isma‘il (AS). And down through the line of that same Isma‘il comes the lineage of the Prophet {{1}}. The one by whose hand the House was built, the Prophet too came from his house.
blocks.77: The Prophet {{1}} himself spoke of his lineage. He said, Allah chose Kinanah from the children of Isma‘il; from Kinanah the Quraysh; from the Quraysh Banu Hashim; and from Banu Hashim me.{{2}}
blocks.78: Choice after choice. The best tribe within the people, the best house within the tribe, and within that house, him.
blocks.79: This lineage was a lineage of honour. Generation after generation they were servants of the Ka‘bah; responsible for the pilgrims’ water and food; leaders of Makkah. None of his forefathers was a slave, none served another as a servant, the lineage bore no stain of illegitimate birth. The Prophet {{1}} said, I came through a line of lawful marriage; no impurity of Jahiliyyah touched me.
blocks.80: In that line, ‘Adnan. Then, crossing many generations, Qusayy ibn Kilab. In Qusayy’s time Makkah was scattered and spread out. He called the tribes together and made them one. He arranged the duty of overseeing the Ka‘bah. He set the rules for running the city. At that time the surroundings of the Arabian Peninsula were like this. In the north-west, towards Sham, the Roman Empire; on its behalf the Arab Christian line of Ghassan managed the desert frontier. In the north-east, towards Iraq, the Persian Empire; on its behalf the Arab line of Hirah, the Lakhmids, managed it. In the east, the coast of the Gulf, from Bahrain to Oman; that too under Persian influence. In the south, Yemen; once the kingdom of Saba’ and Himyar. Around the time of the Prophet’s {{1}} birth it passed first to Abyssinia, then to Persia.
blocks.82: To the south-west Christian Abyssinia; the Kingdom of Axum, who had seized Yemen, and to whose king the Najashi the Companions would later migrate. To the west Egypt; that too part of the Roman Empire, its granary.{{1}}
blocks.83: That is, empires all around, and Arab kings under them. Only in the middle, in Hijaz, in Makkah, Madinah and Ta’if, there is no king; no central state. Makkah was run by the counsel of the tribal chiefs, in Dar al-Nadwah. Qusayy’s descendant Hashim ibn ‘Abd Manaf. From his name the tribe’s name, Banu Hashim.
blocks.84: The line of descent, going backward from the Prophet {{1}}, is this. Muhammad. His father ‘Abdullah. His father ‘Abd al-Muttalib; whose real name was Shaybah. His father Hashim; whose real name was ‘Amr. His father ‘Abd Manaf; whose real name was al-Mughirah. And ‘Abd Manaf’s father was that Qusayy I mentioned just now.{{2}}
blocks.85: The mother’s side is like this too. The Prophet’s {{1}} mother Aminah. Her father Wahb. Wahb’s father ‘Abd Manaf; but this is a different ‘Abd Manaf, this one is the son of Zuhrah. The ‘Abd Manaf of the father’s line was the son of Qusayy; and this one is of Zuhrah. One name, two men.
blocks.86: Wahb’s grandfather Zuhrah. And Zuhrah’s father Kilab ibn Murrah.
blocks.87: This Kilab is the very Kilab of the Prophet’s {{1}} father’s line; Qusayy’s father. That is, Qusayy and Zuhrah were two brothers; the father of both was Kilab. From the father’s side the Prophet {{2}} is a descendant of Qusayy, from the mother’s side of Zuhrah. And at Kilab the two lines become one.{{3}}
blocks.88: From Kilab upward the whole line is of the Quraysh; Murrah, Ka‘b, Lu’ayy, Ghalib, Fihr.
blocks.89: Aminah was, among the Quraysh women of that time, above all in lineage and honour. Her father was the chief of Banu Zuhrah. And ‘Abdullah, Ibn Hisham has said, was the most handsome, the purest, the dearest of ‘Abd al-Muttalib’s sons. Both lines were Quraysh. Both lines were honoured. Nowhere a stain of slavery, nowhere the disgrace of illegitimate birth. The Prophet {{1}} himself said, I am the son of the two sacrificed ones; Isma‘il (AS) and my father ‘Abdullah. Go back five generations and the whole history of Makkah comes into view. This lineage was no outsider to Makkah; Makkah was built by their hands.{{2}}
blocks.90: The habit of boasting of lineage belonged to Arabia. It is ours too.
blocks.91: Whose home is where, what was whose grandfather, how is whose title; in marriage talks these are the very first things raised.
blocks.92: Yet one man of the very lineage whose honour is highest ended the matter.
blocks.93: And he whom his deeds hold back, his lineage cannot move forward.{{1}}
blocks.94: So the family tree is not a paper of honour.
blocks.95: It only shows which house Allah had chosen.
blocks.97: After Hashim, the leadership of Makkah came into ‘Abd al-Muttalib’s hands.
blocks.98: One day in a dream he was told, dig. Where to dig was shown to him too. The place was beside the Ka‘bah; buried under the sand of many ages. People had completely forgotten that one day, beneath the feet of Hajar’s infant, Zamzam had burst forth here.
blocks.99: He took up the spade. People laughed. They obstructed him. With him was only a single son. Digging and digging, one day water rose. The well that had been lost for hundreds of years began again to moisten the throat of Makkah.
blocks.100: But in those days of digging a pain had pierced his chest. All around, everyone had ten or twelve sons. And he had only one. When obstruction came there was no one to stand beside him. Then he made a vow; if Allah gives me ten sons, and they grow up able to protect me, then one of them I will sacrifice in front of the Ka‘bah.
blocks.101: The years rolled on. Ten sons were born. The sons grew up. And the vow came back to mind. The lottery arrows were cast. Whose name came up! ‘Abdullah. The youngest. And the father’s dearest.
blocks.102: The father’s hand trembled. Even so he set out with his son. The people of Makkah ran to the place. The women began to weep. The elders blocked the way. They said, find another way; pay a ransom in camels. Ten camels were set aside and the arrows cast; ‘Abdullah’s name came up. Ten more; again ‘Abdullah. Ten more; again ‘Abdullah. Growing and growing in this way, when the camels reached a hundred, then the arrow moved away from ‘Abdullah’s name.{{1}}
blocks.103: The throat on which the knife had almost come down that day was the same man who a few years later would be the father of the Prophet of the world. ‘Abd al-Muttalib did not know whom he had saved. He thought, I saved my son. In truth he had saved the path of guidance for the whole of mankind.
blocks.104: Even today people make vows. If a son is born I will give this, if illness is cured I will give that, if I get the job I will give this much.
blocks.105: Then the son is born. The illness is cured. The job comes too.
blocks.106: The vow is no longer remembered.
blocks.107: Standing in that dark age, a man had taken up the knife to keep his word.
blocks.108: And we sit forgetting the word given to Allah.

footnotes.0: On Zayd ibn ‘Amr ibn Nufayl see Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith 3826–3828. His going to Syria, hearing the news of the prophet’s coming, and being killed on the way back is narrated in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham.
footnotes.1: On Waraqah ibn Nawfal see Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith 3; on the authority of ‘A’ishah (RA). The long story of Salman al-Farisi (RA) is in Musnad Ahmad, hadith 23737; many scholars of hadith have called it hasan.
footnotes.2: The long story of Salman al-Farisi (RA): Musnad Ahmad, hadith 23737; Ibn Hisham, al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah. Many scholars of hadith have called the report hasan. The three signs: coming to a land of date palms, accepting a gift but not taking charity, and the seal of prophethood between the two shoulders. The ransom (three hundred date saplings and forty uqiyyah of gold) and the Prophet’s {{1}} planting the saplings with his own hands come from the same source.
footnotes.3: Surah al-Baqarah, verse 89. On the waiting and hope of the Jews of Yathrib for the coming of the prophet; the occasion of revelation is narrated in the books of tafsir and Seerah.
footnotes.4: On the speech of Qus ibn Sa‘idah al-Iyadi at ‘Ukaz and the Prophet’s {{1}} saying ‘may Allah have mercy on him’; al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi’s Dala’il al-Nubuwwah. The report is famous, but its chain is weak; it is brought here only to show that ‘people were waiting for a prophet’.
footnotes.5: Sunan Abi Dawud, hadith 4282; Book of the Mahdi. On the authority of ‘Abdullah ibn Mas‘ud (RA). Shaykh al-Albani called it hasan sahih; al-Tirmidhi too narrates a similar report (hadith 2230).
footnotes.6: Sunan Abi Dawud, hadith 4285; Book of the Mahdi. On the authority of Abu Sa‘id al-Khudri (RA). Shaykh al-Albani called it hasan. On the coming of the Mahdi there are several reports in Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah.
footnotes.7: No day or date for the coming of the Mahdi has come in any reliable report. The hadith gives his identity and his work, not the time. Every time in history someone has tried to fix a time or claimed to be the Mahdi, it has been proved false. So only the promise is stated here, not the time.
footnotes.8: Sahih Muslim, hadith 2276; on the authority of Wathilah ibn al-Asqa‘ (RA).
footnotes.9: For the geographical and political condition of the Arabian Peninsula see in detail Safiyy al-Rahman al-Mubarakpuri, al-Raheeq al-Makhtum, chapter ‘Arabia’; on the rulers of Yemen, Hirah and Syria. Persia’s installing a direct governor in Hirah and Persia’s seizure of Yemen were events near the time of the Prophet’s {{1}} birth.
footnotes.10: Among the names, the real name of ‘Abd al-Muttalib is Shaybah, of Hashim ‘Amr, of ‘Abd Manaf al-Mughirah. See Ibn Hisham, al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah; Ibn Sa‘d, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra. The line up to ‘Adnan is established by the consensus of the Ummah; above ‘Adnan, up to Isma‘il (AS), there is a difference of report about the number of names.
footnotes.11: The mother’s line: Aminah bint Wahb ibn ‘Abd Manaf ibn Zuhrah ibn Kilab ibn Murrah. This ‘Abd Manaf ibn Zuhrah is a different person from ‘Abd Manaf ibn Qusayy. See Ibn Hisham, al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah, 1/151–155; al-Raheeq al-Makhtum.
footnotes.12: Sirah of Ibn Hisham, 1/1–125; Ibn Sa‘d, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra; on the lineage and Qusayy ibn Kilab. The lineage of the Prophet {{1}} is agreed up to ‘Adnan; above ‘Adnan, up to Isma‘il (AS), there is a difference of report about the order of names.
footnotes.13: Sahih Muslim, hadith 2699; on the authority of Abu Hurayrah (RA). The last part of a long hadith; narrated on the virtue of knowledge and deeds.
footnotes.14: Sirah of Ibn Hisham, 1/151–160; Ibn Sa‘d, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra; on the digging of Zamzam and the vow. The account is narrated in the Seerah books, not in the hadith collections.

quiz.q: Which sign did the last scholar not mention to Salman al-Farisi about the prophet?
o: He will migrate to a land of date palms
Between his two shoulders will be the seal of prophethood
He will accept a gift, he will not accept charity
He will not speak to anyone
quiz.e: The three signs were: migration to a land of date palms, the seal between the two shoulders, and accepting a gift but not charity. ‘Not speaking’ was no sign.

quiz.q: How did Zayd ibn ‘Amr ibn Nufayl die?
o: Tortured by the Quraysh in Makkah
At the hands of bandits on the way back from Syria
Falling ill beneath the wall of the Ka‘bah
Migrating to Abyssinia and dying there
quiz.e: Going to Syria in search of the truth he got the news that the time of the prophet’s coming had drawn near; on the way back he was killed by bandits. He could not live to see prophethood.

quiz.q: What point does the lesson draw from the story of the hanifs?
o: However dense the darkness, Allah keeps some hearts awake
Becoming Christian was the right path in those days
To know the truth one must leave one’s country
Without a prophet’s coming, guidance is not possible
quiz.e: One searched through books, one wandered from land to land, one stood alone in the desert; Allah kept their hearts awake.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between the hanifs’ search and the Prophet’s ﷺ preparation?
o: They were in Makkah, he was outside Makkah
They were old, he was young
They searched knowingly; he, knowing nothing, was guided by his fitrah
They were alone, he was in a group
quiz.e: Zayd, Waraqah and Salman searched consciously, in books and in travel; the Prophet ﷺ did not yet know he would be a prophet, yet his inner fitrah was keeping him on the right path.

quiz.q: When restless about the truth or the right path, which way does this lesson show?
o: To hold on like the hanifs; if you search, Allah shows the way
To drop the matter and become busy
To accept the opinion of the learned with eyes closed
To wait until a sign is seen
quiz.e: Zayd, Waraqah and Salman did not give up the search even in darkness; Allah guides the searching heart.

quiz.q: What did the Jews of Yathrib say when quarrelling with the Arab tribes?
o: The time of the prophet has come; when he comes we will wipe you out
We are people of the Book, do not quarrel with us, as is generally held
Our Lord is stronger than your Lord
We will soon leave this land
quiz.e: They said, the time of a prophet has come; when he comes we will join him and wipe you out like ‘Ad and Iram. This is mentioned in verse 89 of Surah al-Baqarah.

quiz.q: Who spoke at the fair of ‘Ukaz of the nearness of a prophet’s coming?
o: Waraqah ibn Nawfal
Qus ibn Sa‘idah
Zayd ibn ‘Amr
Bahira the monk
quiz.e: Qus ibn Sa‘idah used to give speeches sitting on a camel; the Prophet ﷺ later said, I saw him at the fair of ‘Ukaz, may Allah have mercy on him. The report is famous, but its chain is weak.

quiz.q: What is the basis of the statement ‘not only the heavens, the earth too was waiting’?
o: There was famine in Makkah, so everyone was waiting for relief, as is generally held
The people of the Book, the monks and the hanifs were all waiting for the prophet
The Quraysh were looking for a new leader
The tribes were looking for a way to stop the wars
quiz.e: The Jews of Yathrib knew a prophet was coming, the monks sat matching the signs, and the hanifs wandered in search of the true religion.

quiz.q: Why did the Jews of Yathrib deny the prophet even though they knew he was coming?
o: He was an Arab, not of Bani Isra’il
The familiar thing came before them, yet they turned away
They wanted to see more signs, as is generally held
Their Book had been lost
quiz.e: According to verse 89 of Surah al-Baqarah, when the recognised thing came they denied it; stubbornness and envy were the cause.

quiz.q: What Qusayy ibn Kilab did for Makkah was
o: Digging the Zamzam well again
Building new settlements and markets around Makkah
Uniting the scattered tribes and setting rules

porbos.title: The Year of the Elephant • Aminah’s House, and an Orphan Before Birth • That Monday Dawn • Which Signs Are Sound, Which Are Not • How Hearsay Spreads • In Halimah’s House • The Chest Was Opened • Loss After Loss • The Child With No One, Even Today • The Days of Tending Sheep • Which Work Is Small

blocks.1: This is from a little before the birth of the Prophet {{1}}.
blocks.2: Abrahah, the ruler of Yemen, built a dazzling church in San‘a’. Plated with gold and silver. From afar it dazzled the eyes. The purpose was not hidden; to draw the pilgrims of Arabia away from the Ka‘bah and toward this place.
blocks.3: But people’s feet did not turn. The pull of the House that Allah Himself has set cannot be bought with gold. Blind with rage, Abrahah set out with an army of elephants. This time not to draw people away; but to break the Ka‘bah and grind it to dust.
blocks.4: On the way he plundered the camels of the people of Makkah. Among them were two hundred of ‘Abd al-Muttalib’s. ‘Abd al-Muttalib went to Abrahah’s tent. Seeing him, Abrahah came down from his throne and showed him respect; he had seen few men of such presence. Then he asked, what do you want?
blocks.5: ‘Abd al-Muttalib said, I want my camels back. Abrahah was astonished. He said, I have come to demolish the house of your religion, and you speak of camels!
blocks.6: History has kept the reply. He said, I am the owner of the camels; so I speak of the camels. And the House has an Owner; He will protect His House.{{1}}
blocks.7: Having said this he came back.
blocks.8: He took hold of the ring on the Ka‘bah’s door and prayed for a while.
blocks.9: Then the people of Makkah left the city and went up to the mountain tops.
blocks.10: The courtyard of the Ka‘bah was left empty.{{1}}
blocks.11: For the House that not one man stood up to save, its Owner Himself stood. What happened then was no longer in human hands. Abrahah’s army halted in the valley of Muhassir between Muzdalifah and Mina. Now the elephant at the front was driven toward the Ka‘bah. The elephant sat down. It was beaten with a stick, it was goaded; it did not rise. Its face was turned toward Yemen; it rose and ran. To the north, to the east, to the west; whichever way it is turned it runs that way. Only when its face is turned toward the Ka‘bah it sits down.
blocks.12: Just then the sky darkened. From the direction of the sea came flocks upon flocks of birds; in bands, one behind another. The Qur’anic word is ‘ababil’; meaning in companies, in flocks. It is not the name of any species of bird.{{1}}
blocks.13: Each one carried three pebbles; one in the beak, two held in the claws of the two feet. The pebbles were small as grains of chickpea. They flew over and began to drop pebbles on the army. Whoever was struck by a pebble, his body was torn apart from within; flesh began to fall away.
blocks.14: The army of sixty thousand was then in headlong flight. One falling upon another. On every road, at every ford, corpses scattered. And Abrahah? He was struck too. Turning back toward San‘a’, his fingers began to fall off one by one. By the time he reached San‘a’ his body had become soft and deformed like a newly hatched chick. At last his chest burst, his heart came out, and he died.{{1}}
blocks.15: And the Quraysh? They had earlier moved away onto the mountainside. When the punishment was over they returned home safely.
blocks.17: Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant? Did He not make their plot go astray? And He sent upon them flocks of birds, which were pelting them with stones of baked clay; and He made them like straw eaten up.{{1}}
blocks.18: The army before which no tribe of Arabia could stand was finished like chewed grass. Birds before the elephant. And the birds won.
blocks.19: The Arabs named that year ‘Am al-Fil; the Year of the Elephant. And in that very year he would be born. That day Allah protected the Ka‘bah with His own hand. Why He did so would be understood a few months later; in the shade of that House His last prophet would grow up. This match is no coincidence. It is arrangement.
blocks.20: The event was not only Makkah’s.
blocks.21: The whole of Arabia trembled that day.
blocks.22: From then on people counted years from this event. So-and-so was born in the Year of the Elephant; so-and-so died so many years after the Year of the Elephant.
blocks.23: And in that very year he came.
blocks.24: Beside the great turning points there often stands a great shaking.
blocks.25: In 1918 a pandemic swept the world. One in every three people was infected. At least fifty million people died; by some estimates a hundred million.
blocks.27: Within a few years the thirteen-hundred-year-old system of the Caliphate collapsed.
blocks.30: Another pandemic came. This time its name was Corona.
blocks.32: ‘Umrah was stopped. The place of tawaf lay empty.{{1}}
blocks.33: Fourteen hundred years ago, in Abrahah’s day too, that courtyard had lain empty in exactly this way.
blocks.34: This time too about fifteen million people died.
blocks.36: What Allah will bring after this, no one knows.{{1}}
blocks.37: In the Year of the Elephant the whole of Arabia trembled.
blocks.38: No one knew that through that very trembling the greatest mercy was coming down.
blocks.39: Aminah’s House, and an Orphan Before Birth
blocks.40: After the vow episode ‘Abd al-Muttalib arranged his son’s marriage. The bride was Aminah bint Wahb of the Banu Zuhrah tribe. Aminah’s father Wahb was the chief of Banu Zuhrah. In lineage and honour no one stood above Aminah among the Quraysh women of that time. Her lineage too joins at Kilab ibn Murrah; exactly where the line of the Prophet’s {{1}} father joins. That is, the child who was coming would be Quraysh from both sides; from both sides of an honoured house.{{2}}
blocks.41: In this house would come the child for whom the heavens and the earth had been waiting.
blocks.42: But Allah’s decree was different. ‘Abdullah had set out on a trading journey. On the way back he fell ill in Madinah. And died right there. His wife was then pregnant. ‘Abdullah left only a little; five camels, a flock of goats, and a slave-girl named Umm Ayman.{{1}}
blocks.43: This Umm Ayman would later raise the child in her arms. The Prophet {{1}} used to call her ‘my mother after my mother’.{{2}}
blocks.44: The child coming into the world would not see his father’s face. And the father could not live to see his son’s face either. An orphan before birth. He on whose shoulders would fall the burden of all mankind, his life begins in the most helpless state.
blocks.46: The Year of the Elephant. The month of Rabi‘ al-Awwal. Monday dawn. In a house in Makkah a child was born.{{1}}
blocks.48: No father. The news went to the grandfather ‘Abd al-Muttalib. The old man came running. He took the child in his arms. Then he took him to the House of the Ka‘bah. Standing there he offered thanks to Allah.
blocks.49: On the seventh day the ‘aqiqah was done. On that very seventh day the grandfather ‘Abd al-Muttalib also had him circumcised; according to the Sunnah of Ibrahim and Isma‘il (peace be upon them).{{1}}
blocks.50: At the naming, people asked, what name did you give? He said, Muhammad. People were astonished. They said, this is not the name of anyone in your lineage! He said, I want Allah to praise him in the heavens, and people to praise him on the earth.{{1}}
blocks.51: What does the name mean? Muhammad; he who is praised again and again. And the name given by his mother was of the same kind; Ahmad. That is, the one who praises most, and the one who is praised most. The name ‘Isa (AS) had foretold is also this Ahmad. The Prophet {{1}} himself mentioned several of his names. He said, I am Muhammad, I am Ahmad, I am al-Mahi; through whom Allah will wipe out disbelief. In the same hadith he named two more; al-Hashir, behind whom people will be gathered on the plain of Gathering, and al-‘Aqib, after whom there is no prophet.{{2}}
blocks.52: There is a match. A man was named ‘the Praised’. And for fourteen hundred years, in the five daily prayers, in every corner of the world, from hundreds of millions of mouths, durood is recited upon him. And the Prophet {{1}} also had a kunyah; Abu al-Qasim. After his eldest son Qasim.{{2}}
blocks.53: It turned out far more than the grandfather had wished.
blocks.54: The grandfather had chosen the name knowing its meaning. Praised; that people might praise him.
blocks.55: And today we choose names because they sound good.
blocks.56: If anyone asks the meaning, we cannot say.
blocks.57: Sometimes we even choose a name that makes us ashamed once we know its meaning.
blocks.58: Yet a name is not unimportant to Allah.
blocks.59: The dearest of your names to Allah are ‘Abdullah and ‘Abd al-Rahman.{{1}}
blocks.60: The Prophet {{1}} himself changed names of bad meaning.
blocks.61: A woman’s name was ‘Asiyah; meaning disobedient. The Prophet {{1}} changed the name to Jamilah.{{2}}
blocks.62: So choosing a beautiful name for a child is part of a father’s responsibility.{{1}}
blocks.63: The child did not choose the name. The father gave it.
blocks.64: The name that will be called all life long, it is surely good to look at its meaning once.
blocks.65: Which Signs Are Sound, Which Are Not
blocks.66: Many signs are in circulation around the birth of the Prophet {{1}}. The fourteen domes of Kisra’s palace collapsing. The thousand-year fire of Persia going out. The lake of Sawah drying up. These things go around gatherings a lot.
blocks.67: But the scholars of hadith have objections to their chains.
blocks.68: The objection is about the narrators. Many of those through whose hands these reports came the scholars of hadith did not hold reliable.{{1}}
blocks.70: The question may arise, then was there no sign of the birth at all? What is proven by a sound chain is itself sufficient. The Prophet {{1}} himself said, I am the supplication of my father Ibrahim, the glad tidings of ‘Isa, and the dream my mother saw; in which she saw that a light came out from her by which the palaces of Syria were lit.{{2}}
blocks.71: A sign occurring before prophethood has a name; irhasat. Those proven by sound or strong chains are in this lesson; the dream of light seen by the mother, the blessing that came down in Halimah’s house, the washing of the chest, the seal of prophethood between the two shoulders. And the greatest irhas is his spotless character for those forty years.
blocks.72: The rest, the ones that are in circulation yet weak or fabricated, I have put a list of in the note; so that you can recognise them when you hear them in gatherings, and be careful when you speak yourself.{{1}}
blocks.73: To raise the Prophet’s {{1}} honour we have no need of weak reports. What is sound is more than enough for his honour. And trying to raise honour with weak reports does the opposite harm. Because one day when someone comes and points out the weakness of that report, the listener’s doubt will not stop at that report alone.
blocks.75: This matter cannot end here. Because the thing is not only about the signs of birth.
blocks.76: A saying is said in a gathering. It sounded good. The listeners sat up. Then that saying went into ten mouths. Not one asked even once, where is this found.
blocks.77: Today the work has become even easier. On a picture it is written, the Prophet {{1}} said. Below, no source. We read. It feels good. We forward it. The job is done in three seconds.
blocks.78: The one who spreads, spreads out of love. No one has bad intent.
blocks.79: The problem is not the intent. The problem is that no one checks whether the saying is truly his.
blocks.80: If the saying is not his, then I have spread in his name something he did not say. And about this he himself has warned. He said, whoever knowingly tells a lie in my name, let him take his place in Hell.{{1}}
blocks.81: This hadith has been narrated by many Companions. Very few sayings of the Seerah have come through so many chains. That is, so many witnesses precisely to show how important the matter is.
blocks.82: Someone may say, I am not knowingly telling a lie; I heard it, so I said it. True. One who does not say it knowingly does not fall under that severe warning. Even so the Prophet {{1}} left one more saying; for all of us. He said, it is enough lying for a person that he relates everything he hears.{{2}}
blocks.83: The saying is not a scolding; it is a measure.
blocks.84: If we spread everything we hear, one day or another a wrong thing too slips out of the mouth. So what is to be done? This very lesson has the model. The palace of Kisra, the extinguished fire, the dried lake; the sayings sound good. But because the chain is weak we did not make them evidence. And the Prophet’s {{1}} honour did not fall short by even that much.
blocks.85: The principle is simple. Fame is no proof. That everyone says it is not a source. And what is sound is more than enough for his honour.
blocks.86: And the work is nothing hard. Next time, before sending any saying in the name of the Prophet {{1}}, ask just one question. Where is this found? If you do not know the answer, do not send it. There is no sin in not sending.
blocks.88: The custom of Arabia was to send city children to villages in the desert. Why? For two reasons. The body would grow strong in the open air. And the pure Arabic of the village would settle on the tongue.
blocks.89: Before being sent to the village, the child was nursed for some days by Suwaybah; a slave-girl of Abu Lahab.{{1}}
blocks.90: Though an uncle, Abu Lahab would later be his greatest enemy. Yet it was his slave-girl who gave him the first milk. Glad at the news of his nephew’s birth, Abu Lahab freed Suwaybah that day. Many years later someone saw Abu Lahab in a dream; after death he is in terrible punishment, but each Monday the punishment is a little lighter; because of that one joy, because of that one act of freeing.{{1}}
blocks.91: That year the wet-nurses of the Banu Sa‘d tribe came to Makkah. A year of famine. Everyone’s eyes were on the well-off children of good houses. Because the more well-off the child’s family, the better the nurse’s payment. No one wanted to take an orphan child. The orphan’s father is not there; who will pay?
blocks.92: When everyone was going back with a child, Halimah al-Sa‘diyyah’s hands were still empty. She said to her husband, I cannot go back empty-handed. Let me take that orphan child. Her husband said, take him. Perhaps Allah has placed blessing in him. Halimah’s mount was also weak; a thin donkey, and a she-camel whose udder had not a drop of milk. In those same empty hands she lifted the orphan child into her arms.
blocks.93: Halimah (RA) later said herself that what happened next she had never seen in her life. The she-camel whose milk had dried, her udder filled. The little ones who used to cry all night with hunger, slept with full bellies. In the land where there was no grass, their animals returned full from the very same place. People of the tribe began to say to one another, graze your animals where Halimah’s animals graze.{{1}}
blocks.94: The one whom people had thought a burden and left aside, in the house of the one who went home with him, blessing came down. The orphan whom no one wanted became the cause of good for the whole tribe.
blocks.96: Which relative is advantageous to take into the house, which boy is worth educating because he will be useful later.
blocks.97: Whoever seems a burden, we pass by.
blocks.98: Halimah too had passed him by at first.
blocks.99: Because she would have to go back empty-handed, in the end it was she who took him up.
blocks.101: The one we leave aside thinking him a burden, perhaps the blessing of the house comes at his hand!
blocks.103: In Halimah’s house itself an event took place, which is narrated in Sahih Muslim.
blocks.104: The child Muhammad {{1}} was playing with the other boys. Suddenly two strangers came. They laid him down. Then they split open his chest. From inside they took out a black clot of blood and threw it away. They said, this was Satan’s share. Then they washed the heart in Zamzam water and put it back in its place.{{2}}
blocks.105: The playmates ran to the foster-mother with the news. They said, Muhammad has been killed! Everyone ran there. They saw him standing. Only his face was pale. Anas (RA) says, I saw the mark of the stitching on his chest. And another mark remained between the two shoulders; a little piece of raised flesh like a pigeon’s egg. Its name is the seal of prophethood. Many Companions saw it with their own eyes; some even touched it with their hand.{{1}}
blocks.106: What is the significance of this event? The heart on which revelation would descend was being washed and made ready beforehand. Forty years before. Before building a house people clean the foundation. And here the foundation is being cleaned by Allah’s own arrangement.
blocks.108: Let the inside be as it is; we keep piling deeds on top.
blocks.109: Prayers increase, fasts increase, tasbih increases.
blocks.110: And inside, envy remains just as it was.
blocks.112: However high a wall is raised without cleaning the foundation, one day it leans and falls.
blocks.114: The child was then six. His mother Aminah took him to Madinah; to visit her husband’s grave, and to show him to the relatives. In Madinah were Aminah’s maternal uncles’ clan, Banu ‘Adi ibn al-Najjar. Having spent a few days there they set out on the way back. On the way, at a place called Abwa’, the mother fell ill. And died right there.{{1}}
blocks.115: A child of six. He had never seen his father. And his mother he lost on the desert road, on the way back. The road on which two had gone, one returned. The slave-girl Umm Ayman carried the child in her arms back to Makkah.{{1}}
blocks.116: The grandfather ‘Abd al-Muttalib took him to his chest. The old man loved his grandson so much that on the bed spread for him in the shade of the Ka‘bah, even his own sons could not sit. And the grandson would come and sit straight down there. If anyone tried to move him, the grandfather said, leave him; this grandson of mine has great honour.
blocks.117: Two years later the grandfather too was gone. He was then eight. Now the uncle Abu Talib took responsibility. He raised his nephew like his own child. And stood beside him all his life. One incident comes in the Seerah books. Once when drought struck Makkah, Abu Talib took his little nephew along and made the istisqa’; and rain came down. The chain of the report is weak; but a line of verse by Abu Talib has become famous, whose meaning is; that radiant face, by whose means rain is asked of the clouds.{{1}}
blocks.118: The calculation is this. Before birth, the father. At six, the mother. At eight, the grandfather. He who would one day be the guardian of the whole Ummah, in childhood not one guardian of his own lasted. And many years later Allah would remind him of that childhood—
blocks.120: Did He not find you an orphan and give you refuge? And He found you unaware of the way, and guided you. And He found you in need, and made you self-sufficient.{{1}}
blocks.121: The man who tasted the pain of the orphan himself, by his hand Allah would have the orphan’s rights written. This too is arrangement.
blocks.122: The Child With No One, Even Today
blocks.123: The child you have heard of so far lost his father before birth, his mother at six, his grandfather at eight.
blocks.124: In your own neighbourhood too there is such a child. No father. The mother works in other people’s houses. He does not go to school; he works in a shop. You see him every day. You do not know his name.
blocks.125: By orphan we understand the orphanage. When Ramadan comes we give a donation. At Eid we feed them once. The deed is good. But what the Prophet {{1}} said is a different thing.
blocks.126: He said, I and the one who cares for an orphan will be in Paradise like this. Then he joined two fingers to show.{{1}}
blocks.127: The word is important here. He did not say, the one who gives money to an orphan. He said, the one who is the guardian of an orphan. Money can be given from a distance. To be a guardian you have to go near.
blocks.128: And the language in which Allah said it in the Qur’an is even harder.
blocks.130: So do not be harsh with the orphan. And do not scold the one who asks for help.{{1}}
blocks.131: To whom is this being said? To the one who was himself an orphan. The one who knows what it means not to see a father’s face. Even he was reminded. And we!
blocks.132: If Allah had wished He could have given His last prophet birth in a royal palace. He did not. He on whose shoulders would fall the burden of all mankind, He started in the most helpless state. Because the one who does not know hunger himself will not understand the hungry.
blocks.133: So take one task from today’s lesson. The orphan child who is around you, this week find out his name. Just the name. Knowing the name means coming to know the person. And one whom you know, you can no longer pass by.
blocks.135: In his youth he used to tend sheep around Makkah. He himself said, Allah has sent no prophet who did not tend sheep. The Companions asked, you too? He said, yes; I too tended the sheep of the people of Makkah for a few qirats.{{1}}
blocks.136: The question is, why does this work come again and again in the lives of prophets? The reason is hidden inside the work itself. Handling a flock of sheep is no easy work. They scatter. One goes this way, another that way. The shepherd has to watch each, yet cannot use force on any. Patience is needed. A gentle hand is needed. And from afar one has to keep an eye on the whole flock.
blocks.137: Leading a people is exactly the same. Allah trained His prophets for leadership with a flock of sheep. Not in a palace. In the open fields of the desert.
blocks.138: And the work has another side. In that society tending sheep was a lowly work. The grandson of the tribe’s chief doing this work! He did it. And later said it with his own mouth. The one who did not count even lowly work as shame for the sake of lawful livelihood is our Prophet.
blocks.140: Now let us look at ourselves. In our society there is a measure of work; it is not written, yet everyone knows.
blocks.141: If a son sits the BCS, pride. If a son opens a shop, silence. If a son takes up a mason’s work, hiding it. If anyone asks, it is said, he is doing something.
blocks.142: Yet what should the question have been? Whether the money is lawful. That question we do not ask. We ask, what will people say.
blocks.143: The grandson of Makkah’s tribal chief tended sheep. In that society it was lowly work; the work of slaves and the poor. He did it. And the biggest thing, he did not hide it. Years and years later, before the Companions, he said it with his own mouth, I too tended the sheep of the people of Makkah; for a few qirats.
blocks.144: Who is saying this? He was then the head of state in Madinah. If he wished he could have suppressed that chapter of his life. No one would even have known. He said it.
blocks.145: And we! We hide our father’s occupation. In marriage talks we say, he does business; actually he drives a rickshaw-van. Our own old days of hardship we tell no one. As if they were stains, not identity.
blocks.146: A job is not small. A job becomes small if its money is unlawful. And by that reckoning, a flock of sheep stands higher than an office chair built on bribe money.
blocks.147: Now settle one task. The work you feel ashamed to do, yet lawful; this week confess it to at least one person. You will see the burden has come down.

footnotes.14: The proof that the day of birth was Monday is in Sahih Muslim, hadith 1162; on the authority of Abu Qatadah (RA). footnotes.15: On circumcision there are three reports: (a) born already circumcised; (b) done by the grandfather ‘Abd al-Muttalib on the seventh day; (c) in Halimah’s house (weak). The first two are well known and acceptable. See Ibn Sa‘d, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra; Ibn al-Qayyim, Tuhfat al-Mawdud.
footnotes.16: Sirah of Ibn Hisham, 1/159–160; Ibn Sa‘d, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra; on the naming. The account is narrated in the books of Seerah.
footnotes.17: Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith 3532; Sahih Muslim, hadith 2354; on the authority of Jubayr ibn Mut‘im (RA).

footnotes.19: Sahih Muslim, hadith 2132; on the authority of Ibn ‘Umar (RA).

footnotes.21: The list of ‘a father’s duties toward his child’, such as ‘choosing a beautiful name, teaching good manners’, current in da‘wah gatherings, is chiefly a summing up by the jurists. The chain of the well-known original report (‘Haqq al-walad ‘ala al-walid an yuhsina ismahu…’) is weak; so it is not brought here as evidence. The point about the duty stands on sound reports: the hadith of the names dearest to Allah (note 465) and the Prophet’s {{1}} own practice of changing names (note 466).
footnotes.22: Imam al-Bukhari (RH) said, ‘I have put nothing in my Jami‘ except what is sound; and I left out many sound hadith for fear of length.’ Khatib al-Baghdadi, Tarikh Baghdad; Ibn Hajar, Hady al-Sari (introduction to Fath al-Bari). So that a report is not in Sahih al-Bukhari or Sahih Muslim is no proof that it is weak. A great portion of sound hadith is in Sunan Abi Dawud, Jami‘ al-Tirmidhi, Sunan al-Nasa’i, Sunan Ibn Majah, Musnad Ahmad, Sahih Ibn Khuzaymah and Sahih Ibn Hibban. In judging the grade one must look at the chain, not at the location.
footnotes.23: These signs are narrated in al-Bayhaqi’s Dala’il al-Nubuwwah and in the history books; the scholars of hadith have given the opinion that the chain is weak. See ‘Allamah Shibli Nu‘mani, Sirat al-Nabi; the notes of ‘Allamah Safiyy al-Rahman al-Mubarakpuri’s al-Raheeq al-Makhtum.
footnotes.24: Musnad Ahmad, hadith 17150; Ibn Hibban; on the authority of al-‘Irbad ibn Sariyah (RA). Many scholars of hadith have called the report hasan.
footnotes.25: Other events about the birth and childhood of the Prophet {{1}} that are widely current in da‘wah gatherings, yet not proven by a sound chain; the chain weak, some fabricated: (1) falling in prostration at the moment of birth, or raising a finger and looking at the sky; (2) all the idols of the Ka‘bah falling on their faces on the night of birth; (3) Satan’s cry of anguish; (4) the fourteen domes of Kisra’s palace collapsing, the thousand-year fire-temple of Persia going out, the lake of Sawah drying up; (5) Halimah’s donkey suddenly becoming swift; (6) the detailed conversation of Bahira and Nastura the monk; (7) the shade of two angels that Maysarah saw and the tree bending down; (8) the wrestling with Rukanah the wrestler. These are famous, yet it is safest to avoid them in da‘wah discussions. See Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah; Mubarakpuri, the notes of al-Raheeq al-Makhtum; Nasir al-Din al-Albani, Silsilat al-Ahadith al-Da‘ifah.
footnotes.26: Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith 110; Sahih Muslim, Muqaddimah. Narrated on the authority of many Companions including Anas, Abu Hurayrah and al-Mughirah ibn Shu‘bah (RA); the report is mutawatir.
footnotes.27: Sahih Muslim, Muqaddimah; on the authority of Abu Hurayrah (RA). A similar report is in Sunan Abi Dawud, hadith 4992 too.
footnotes.28: On the first nursing, Ibn Sa‘d, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra 1/108–109. On Suwaybah’s nursing, Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Marriage, hadith 5101.
footnotes.29: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Marriage, hadith 5101 and related reports; on the authority of ‘Urwah (RA). The incident is narrated as a dream; not evidence in creed, but preserved by a sound chain.
footnotes.30: Sirah of Ibn Hisham, 1/162–166; Ibn Sa‘d, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra; the account of Halimah al-Sa‘diyyah. The account is narrated in the books of Seerah.
footnotes.31: Sahih Muslim, hadith 162; on the authority of Anas ibn Malik (RA).
footnotes.32: Sahih Muslim, Book of Virtues, hadith 2344 (Jabir ibn Samurah); Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith 3541 and 190 (al-Sa’ib ibn Yazid; he himself touched the seal of prophethood).
footnotes.33: Sirah of Ibn Hisham, 1/168; Ibn Sa‘d, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra. Later the Prophet {{1}} visited his mother’s grave; Sahih Muslim, hadith 976.
footnotes.34: Sirah of Ibn Hisham, 1/168; Ibn Sa‘d, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra 1/116–117. Aminah (RA) went to Madinah, to her maternal uncles’ clan Banu ‘Adi ibn al-Najjar; on the way back she died at Abwa’. The slave-girl Umm Ayman brought the child back to Makkah.
footnotes.35: Sirah of Ibn Hisham, 1/176; Ibn Kathir, al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah. The chain of this account of Abu Talib’s praying for rain with the child Prophet {{1}} is weak; but Abu Talib’s line ‘wa abyada yustasqa al-ghamamu bi-wajhihi’ is well known in the Seerah books.
footnotes.37: Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith 5304 and 6005; on the authority of Sahl ibn Sa‘d (RA). The Prophet {{1}} showed by joining the index and middle fingers.
